title: What Happens to Your Body in Space Without a Suit?
sources: Christopher S. Baird (physics professor, West Texas A&M University), 'How long can a human in outer space last without a spacesuit before exploding?', Science Questions with Surprising Answers, 2012-12-17 ('Humans exposed to the vacuum of space don't explode'; 'our tissue is strong enough to handle the imbalance'; citing FAA AC 61-107, people remain fully conscious and useful for 9-12 seconds after vacuum exposure; they die from lack of oxygen): https://wtamu.edu/~cbaird/sq/2012/12/17/how-long-can-a-human-in-outer-space-last-without-a-spacesuit-before-exploding/

Michael Barratt (NASA astronaut and physician), 'The Body at Vacuum', The Engines of Our Ingenuity No. 2691, University of Houston (water's vapor pressure at body temperature is about 1/16 of an atmosphere, so above ~63,000 ft body fluids boil (ebullism); moist surfaces such as the eyes, mouth, throat and airways are affected immediately; vapor forms beneath the skin and in venous blood; Joe Kittinger's hand swelled to about twice its size after a glove pressure failure; about 12 seconds of useful consciousness; in 1966 a technician in a suit-test chamber lost suit pressure, recalled the sensation of saliva boiling off his tongue before losing consciousness, the chamber was quickly repressurized and he 'went home for lunch'; end note names him as NASA engineer James LeBlanc, chamber repressurized in 87 seconds): https://engines.egr.uh.edu/episode/2691

Guinness World Records, 'Highest equivalent altitude exposure survived' (Jim LeBlanc, NASA volunteer test subject testing space suits, 14 December 1966, depressurisation chamber in Houston, Texas; equipment failure disconnected the hose that kept his suit pressurised, exposing him to the equivalent of 120,000 ft; chamber took 87 seconds to repressurise, when he regained consciousness; he recalled his saliva boiling off his tongue just before he passed out; no long-term effects): https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/447311-highest-equivalent-altitude-exposure-survived

Tease (next video): Guinness World Records, 'Longest attack of hiccups' (Charles Osborne, USA, started hiccupping in 1922 while weighing a hog before slaughter and continued until February 1990, about 68 years; Smithsonian Magazine 'The Curious Case of Charles Osborne, Who Hiccuped for 68 Years Straight' confirms 1922-1990): https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/67619-longest-attack-of-hiccups

Tease (next video): Cleveland Clinic, 'Hiccups' (repeated spasms of the diaphragm; the glottis snaps shut, making the 'hic' sound; persistent hiccups last longer than 48 hours): https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/17672-hiccups

lines.text: What happens to your body in space without a suit?
lines.caps: WHAT *HAPPENS | TO YOUR *BODY | IN *SPACE | WITHOUT A *SUIT?

lines.text: Spoiler, you don't explode. Your skin's too tough.
But the weird part starts in your mouth.
With almost no pressure, water boils at body temperature,
so your eyes and tongue start to fizz,
With no oxygen, you black out in about twelve seconds.
lines.caps: WITH NO *OXYGEN | YOU *BLACK OUT | IN *ABOUT | *12 SECONDS

lines.text: In nineteen sixty-six, a NASA tester's suit hose came loose
inside a vacuum chamber in Houston.
His last memory? Spit boiling off his tongue.
The air came back, he woke up, and went home for lunch.
lines.caps: THE *AIR | CAME *BACK | HE *WOKE UP | AND WENT *HOME | FOR *LUNCH

lines.text: No explosion, just a twelve second countdown.
